title: Mastering Linux File Permissions
markdown:
# Mastering Linux File Permissions

Every file on a Linux system carries a small but powerful set of labels: who owns it, which group it belongs to, and what each category of user is allowed to do with it. Get these right, and you have a system where people can collaborate freely without stepping on each other's work. Linux gives you three tools to control this. `umask` decides what permissions new files start with. `chmod` changes permissions on files that already exist. `setfacl` goes further, letting you assign different permissions to multiple users and groups on the same file — something the basic model can't do alone.

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/1bc572d6354bd0f165f066ab72b933a5a47457f7/Linux%20Labs/Lab%2007/images/permission-model.svg)

By the end of this lab, you will be able to:

- Read and interpret Linux file permission strings (`rwxr-xr-x`)
- Use `umask` to control default permissions on newly created files
- Use `chmod` to set specific permissions using both symbolic and octal notation
- Use `setfacl` to apply per-user and per-group access control lists
- Use `getfacl` to verify and audit ACL settings
- Apply the principle of least privilege in a real multi-team project setup

## The Scenario: ProjectX at Poridhi.io

You are a system administrator at `Poridhi.io`. The development team is launching a new project called **ProjectX** with three teams that each need different levels of access:

| Team | Group | What they need |
|------|-------|----------------|
| Developers | `dev` | Full access to source code, read-only on config files |
| Operations | `ops` | Full access to config files, read-only on source code |
| QA Testers | `qa` | Read-only everywhere, write access only in the tests directory |

A single `chmod` assignment can't express three different rules for three different groups on the same directory. By the end of this lab, you will have built this exact setup — correctly and verifiably.

## Part 1: Understanding the Linux Permission Model

Before touching any commands, let's understand what we're working with.

### How Permissions Are Displayed

Run `ls -l` on any file and you'll see a string like this:

```
-rwxr-xr--  1  alice  dev  4096  Mar 10 09:00  deploy.sh
```

The first 10 characters are the permission string:

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/1bc572d6354bd0f165f066ab72b933a5a47457f7/Linux%20Labs/Lab%2007/images/permissions.svg)

Each triplet uses three characters: `r` (read), `w` (write), `x` (execute). A `-` means that permission is not granted.

### The Three Tools and How They Relate

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/1bc572d6354bd0f165f066ab72b933a5a47457f7/Linux%20Labs/Lab%2007/images/Tools.svg)

| Tool | When it acts | What it controls |
|------|-------------|-----------------|
| `umask` | At file creation time | Removes permissions from the default before the file exists |
| `chmod` | On existing files | Sets or changes permissions on files and directories |
| `setfacl` | On existing files | Extends permissions beyond the single owner/group model |

Think of it this way: `umask` is the factory setting, `chmod` is the manual adjustment, and `setfacl` is the fine-tuning that the basic model can't handle.

## Part 2: Setting Up the Environment

### Step 1: Install the ACL Package

`setfacl` and `getfacl` come from the `acl` package, which may not be installed by default:

```bash
sudo apt update && sudo apt install -y acl
```

Verify the tools are available:

```bash
which setfacl getfacl
```

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/1bc572d6354bd0f165f066ab72b933a5a47457f7/Linux%20Labs/Lab%2007/images/image.png)

### Step 2: Create Groups and Users

Let's create the three teams and their users:

```bash
# Create groups
sudo groupadd dev
sudo groupadd ops
sudo groupadd qa
```

```bash
# Create users for each group
sudo useradd -m -s /bin/bash dev_user1
sudo useradd -m -s /bin/bash dev_user2
sudo useradd -m -s /bin/bash ops_user1
sudo useradd -m -s /bin/bash ops_user2
sudo useradd -m -s /bin/bash qa_user1
sudo useradd -m -s /bin/bash qa_user2
```

```bash
# Set passwords for all users
sudo passwd dev_user1
sudo passwd dev_user2
sudo passwd ops_user1
sudo passwd ops_user2
sudo passwd qa_user1
sudo passwd qa_user2
```

```bash
# Add users to their groups
sudo usermod -aG dev dev_user1
sudo usermod -aG dev dev_user2
sudo usermod -aG ops ops_user1
sudo usermod -aG ops ops_user2
sudo usermod -aG qa qa_user1
sudo usermod -aG qa qa_user2
```

Verify the groups and membership:

```bash
getent group dev
getent group ops
getent group qa
```

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/1bc572d6354bd0f165f066ab72b933a5a47457f7/Linux%20Labs/Lab%2007/images/image-1.png)

```bash
id dev_user1
id ops_user1
id qa_user1
```

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/1bc572d6354bd0f165f066ab72b933a5a47457f7/Linux%20Labs/Lab%2007/images/image-2.png)

**Why it matters**: Users can belong to multiple groups, but each file has exactly one group owner. `setfacl` is what lets us break out of that limitation later.

### Step 3: Create the Directory Structure

```bash
mkdir -p /home/poridhian/code/projects/ProjectX/src
mkdir -p /home/poridhian/code/projects/ProjectX/config
mkdir -p /home/poridhian/code/projects/ProjectX/docs
mkdir -p /home/poridhian/code/projects/ProjectX/tests
```

Verify the structure:

```bash
ls -lR /home/poridhian/code/projects/ProjectX
```

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/1bc572d6354bd0f165f066ab72b933a5a47457f7/Linux%20Labs/Lab%2007/images/image-3.png)

The `-p` flag creates all parent directories in one command. We now have four subdirectories, each representing a distinct area of the project with different access requirements.

## Part 3: Default Permissions with `umask`

### Step 1: Check the Current umask

```bash
umask
```

You will likely see `0022`. This value tells the system which permission bits to *remove* from every new file or directory at creation time.

Here is how the calculation works:

| | Files (max 666) | Directories (max 777) |
|-|----------------|----------------------|
| Default max | `rw-rw-rw-` (666) | `rwxrwxrwx` (777) |
| umask 022 removes | `----w--w-` (022) | `----w--w-` (022) |
| Result | `rw-r--r--` (644) | `rwxr-xr-x` (755) |

> **Note:** Files never get execute permission by default, even with umask 000. This is a Linux safety feature — a file must be explicitly made executable.

### Step 2: Create a File and Check Its Permissions

```bash
touch /tmp/testfile
ls -l /tmp/testfile
```

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/1bc572d6354bd0f165f066ab72b933a5a47457f7/Linux%20Labs/Lab%2007/images/image-4.png)

The file has `rw-r--r--` (644) — exactly what umask 022 produces. Now let's see what a more restrictive umask does.

### Step 3: Set a Stricter umask for the Project

For ProjectX, we want new files to be group-readable but hidden from others. umask `027` achieves this:

| | Files | Directories |
|-|-------|-------------|
| umask 027 result | `rw-r-----` (640) | `rwxr-x---` (750) |

Create a project environment script that team members source when working on the project:

```bash
cat > /home/poridhian/code/projects/ProjectX/project_env.sh << 'EOF'
#!/bin/bash
# Set project-specific umask
umask 027
echo "ProjectX environment active"
echo "umask is now: $(umask)"
EOF

chmod +x /home/poridhian/code/projects/ProjectX/project_env.sh
```

Test it:

```bash
source /home/poridhian/code/projects/ProjectX/project_env.sh
```

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/1bc572d6354bd0f165f066ab72b933a5a47457f7/Linux%20Labs/Lab%2007/images/image-5.png)

```bash
touch /tmp/testfile_027
ls -l /tmp/testfile_027
```

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/1bc572d6354bd0f165f066ab72b933a5a47457f7/Linux%20Labs/Lab%2007/images/image-6.png)

The new file has `rw-r-----` (640) — others have no access at all.

> **Note:** `umask` changes only apply to the current shell session. Team members must `source` (not execute) the script to inherit the setting.

**Why it matters**: Setting the right umask means files are born with safe defaults. Without it, every developer would need to manually `chmod` every file they create — and they won't always remember.

## Part 4: Setting Base Permissions with `chmod`

### Step 1: Set Project Directory Ownership

First, assign the top-level ownership to `dev_user1` with `dev` as the group, since developers need the broadest base access:

```bash
sudo chown -R dev_user1:dev /home/poridhian/code/projects/ProjectX
```

Verify:

```bash
ls -la /home/poridhian/code/projects/ProjectX
```

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/1bc572d6354bd0f165f066ab72b933a5a47457f7/Linux%20Labs/Lab%2007/images/image-7.png)

The `-R` flag applies the change recursively to all files and subdirectories.

### Step 2: Set Permissions per Directory

Now set base permissions for each subdirectory based on the team requirements:

```bash
# Root project directory — owner and group full access, others can read
sudo chmod 775 /home/poridhian/code/projects/ProjectX

# Source code — owner and group only, others locked out
sudo chmod 770 /home/poridhian/code/projects/ProjectX/src

# Config — owner and group only, others locked out
sudo chmod 770 /home/poridhian/code/projects/ProjectX/config

# Docs — everyone can read, owner and group can write
sudo chmod 775 /home/poridhian/code/projects/ProjectX/docs

# Tests — everyone can read, owner and group can write
sudo chmod 775 /home/poridhian/code/projects/ProjectX/tests
```

Here is what `chmod` notation means:

| Digit | Who | Permission |
|-------|-----|-----------|
| First | Owner (u) | 7 = rwx |
| Second | Group (g) | 7 = rwx, 5 = r-x, 0 = --- |
| Third | Others (o) | 5 = r-x, 0 = --- |

### Step 3: Verify with ls -la

```bash
ls -la /home/poridhian/code/projects/ProjectX/
```

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/1bc572d6354bd0f165f066ab72b933a5a47457f7/Linux%20Labs/Lab%2007/images/image-8.png)

You can also use symbolic notation to make targeted changes. For example, to add execute permission for the group on a specific file:

```bash
# Symbolic: add execute for group
sudo chmod g+x /home/poridhian/code/projects/ProjectX/src

# Symbolic: remove write for others
sudo chmod o-w /home/poridhian/code/projects/ProjectX/docs

# Symbolic: set others to read-only exactly
sudo chmod o=r /home/poridhian/code/projects/ProjectX/docs
```

**Why it matters**: `chmod` with octal notation is fast for setting all three categories at once. Symbolic notation is better when you want to add or remove a single bit without disturbing the rest.

## Part 5: Fine-Grained Control with `setfacl`

`chmod` lets you set one group per file. But ProjectX has three groups, each needing different access on the same directories. This is exactly what ACLs are designed for.

### Step 1: Understand the setfacl Syntax

```bash
# Format: setfacl -m [type]:[name]:[permissions] [path]
# type: u (user) or g (group)

# Give a specific user read access
setfacl -m u:alice:r file.txt

# Give a group read and write access
setfacl -m g:marketing:rw file.txt

# Apply recursively with -R
setfacl -R -m g:marketing:rw directory/
```

### Step 2: Apply ACLs for the `src` Directory

Developers own it. Operations need read-only. QA needs read-only:

```bash
# ops: read + execute on src (read-only, x needed to enter the directory)
sudo setfacl -R -m g:ops:rx /home/poridhian/code/projects/ProjectX/src

# qa: read + execute on src
sudo setfacl -R -m g:qa:rx /home/poridhian/code/projects/ProjectX/src
```

### Step 3: Apply ACLs for the `config` Directory

Operations own the config. Developers need read-only access:

```bash
# ops: full access to config
sudo setfacl -R -m g:ops:rwx /home/poridhian/code/projects/ProjectX/config

# dev: read-only on config
sudo setfacl -R -m g:dev:rx /home/poridhian/code/projects/ProjectX/config

# qa: read-only on config
sudo setfacl -R -m g:qa:rx /home/poridhian/code/projects/ProjectX/config
```

### Step 4: Apply ACLs for the `tests` Directory

QA needs write access here, read-only everywhere else:

```bash
# qa: full access to tests
sudo setfacl -R -m g:qa:rwx /home/poridhian/code/projects/ProjectX/tests
```

### Step 5: Verify with `getfacl`

```bash
getfacl /home/poridhian/code/projects/ProjectX/src
```

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/1bc572d6354bd0f165f066ab72b933a5a47457f7/Linux%20Labs/Lab%2007/images/image-9.png)

```bash
getfacl /home/poridhian/code/projects/ProjectX/config
```

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/1bc572d6354bd0f165f066ab72b933a5a47457f7/Linux%20Labs/Lab%2007/images/image-10.png)

```bash
getfacl /home/poridhian/code/projects/ProjectX/tests
```

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/1bc572d6354bd0f165f066ab72b933a5a47457f7/Linux%20Labs/Lab%2007/images/image-11.png)

`getfacl` shows the full ACL — including both the standard `chmod` permissions and any extended entries added by `setfacl`. When a file has ACL entries beyond the base owner/group/others, `ls -l` marks it with a `+` at the end of the permission string (e.g., `drwxrwx---+`).

**Why it matters**: Without ACLs you'd have to pick one group as the file's group owner, then create nested group hierarchies or shared accounts to work around the limitation. ACLs let you express the real access model — no workarounds needed.

## Part 6: Create Test Files and Verify Access

### Step 1: Create Test Files in Each Directory

Now, create files in each directory:

```bash
echo "// Main application logic" > /home/poridhian/code/projects/ProjectX/src/main.c
echo "db_host=db-01" > /home/poridhian/code/projects/ProjectX/config/app.conf
echo "# Documentation" > /home/poridhian/code/projects/ProjectX/docs/README.md
echo "test_case_1: pass" > /home/poridhian/code/projects/ProjectX/tests/test1.txt
```

> **Note:** You should get `Permission denied` in the response. Do you understand why?

The directories are now owned by `dev_user1:dev`. Your current shell session runs as `poridhian`, who is not in the `dev` group — so plain redirection (`>`) will be denied. This is the permission model working correctly.

To create files inside these directories, run the commands as `dev_user1` using `sudo -u`:

```bash
sudo -u dev_user1 bash -c 'echo "// Main application logic" > /home/poridhian/code/projects/ProjectX/src/main.c'
sudo -u dev_user1 bash -c 'echo "db_host=db-01" > /home/poridhian/code/projects/ProjectX/config/app.conf'
sudo -u dev_user1 bash -c 'echo "# Documentation" > /home/poridhian/code/projects/ProjectX/docs/README.md'
sudo -u dev_user1 bash -c 'echo "test_case_1: pass" > /home/poridhian/code/projects/ProjectX/tests/test1.txt'
```

> **Note:** The `bash -c` wrapper is necessary here because the shell performs the `>` redirection — not the command itself. Without it, `sudo` elevates only `echo`, while the redirection still runs as your current user and gets denied.

Verify the files were created:

```bash
ls -la /home/poridhian/code/projects/ProjectX/src/
ls -la /home/poridhian/code/projects/ProjectX/config/
```

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/1bc572d6354bd0f165f066ab72b933a5a47457f7/Linux%20Labs/Lab%2007/images/image-12.png)

### Step 2: Test Access as a Developer

```bash
# Should succeed — devs have full access to src
sudo -u dev_user1 cat /home/poridhian/code/projects/ProjectX/src/main.c

# Should succeed — devs can read config (ACL grants rx)
sudo -u dev_user1 cat /home/poridhian/code/projects/ProjectX/config/app.conf

# Should succeed — dev_user1 is the file owner, owner permissions apply before any ACL
sudo -u dev_user1 bash -c 'echo "new_setting=true" >> /home/poridhian/code/projects/ProjectX/config/app.conf'
```

> **Note — 3rd command:** The ACL restricts `dev` to read-only on `config/`, so writing should fail — but it succeeds. `dev_user1` is the file **owner** (they created it in Step 1). Linux checks **owner first**, before any ACL entry, so `dev_user1` gets owner-level `rw` access regardless of the ACL.

### Step 3: Test Access as an Operations User

```bash
# Should succeed — ops can read src (ACL grants rx)
sudo -u ops_user1 cat /home/poridhian/code/projects/ProjectX/src/main.c

# Should fail — ops has read-only on src
sudo -u ops_user1 bash -c 'echo "// ops edit" >> /home/poridhian/code/projects/ProjectX/src/main.c'

# Should fail — file has no ACL, ops_user1 is "others" on the file with read-only
sudo -u ops_user1 bash -c 'echo "db_port=5432" >> /home/poridhian/code/projects/ProjectX/config/app.conf'
```

> **Note — 3rd command:** The ACL gives `ops` full access to `config/`, so writing should succeed — but it fails. `setfacl -R` ran before `app.conf` existed, so the file has **no ACL**. `ops_user1` falls under **others** on the file (owned by `dev_user1`, permissions `644`), which is read-only.

### Step 4: Test Access as a QA User

```bash
# Should succeed — qa has read-only on src
sudo -u qa_user1 cat /home/poridhian/code/projects/ProjectX/src/main.c

# Should fail — qa has read-only on src
sudo -u qa_user1 bash -c 'echo "// qa edit" >> /home/poridhian/code/projects/ProjectX/src/main.c'

# Should fail — file has no ACL, qa_user1 is "others" on the file with read-only
sudo -u qa_user1 bash -c 'echo "test_case_2: pass" >> /home/poridhian/code/projects/ProjectX/tests/test1.txt'
```

> **Note — 3rd command:** The ACL gives `qa` full access to `tests/`, so writing should succeed — but it fails. Same reason as Step 3 — `setfacl -R` ran before `test1.txt` existed, so the file has **no ACL** and `qa_user1` falls under **others** (read-only).

Each test confirms that the permission model is working exactly as designed. The `sudo -u` flag runs a command as a specific user without needing to log in as them — useful for testing access in a controlled way.

## Conclusion

In this lab, we built a real multi-team access control system from scratch. We used three tools in combination — each handling what the others can't:

- `umask` set safe defaults so new files never started with too many permissions
- `chmod` set the base layer of access per directory for the owning group
- `setfacl` added the extra layer that `chmod` alone cannot express — different permissions for multiple groups on the same files

The pattern here, applying permissions in layers from broad to specific, is the standard approach in any Linux environment where more than one team shares a filesystem.
